analysis.title: NEPC Asset Allocation Roundtable, The 2026 Edition
key_insights: Midterm results matched the polls at the federal level, but the swing in state legislative and governor races was larger than expected. War fatigue, gas prices and local opposition to data centers (Texas, Georgia, Ohio) were cited as factors.

NEPC expects little legislative progress over the next two years. Divided government is generally favorable for US equities, but markets will begin to discount a range of 2028 election outcomes, which could add volatility.

Data-center politics: state and local officials can pause or delay projects. NEPC expects the AI buildout to slow somewhat, not stop. Regulation is named as the biggest overhang on AI investment pace.

AI earnings growth will become more selective. Memory is cited as an area where high returns attract competitors and the current growth pace is unlikely to persist. Other AI areas protected by physical constraints may hold up better.

Participants see the AI buildout as early (first or second inning). A meaningful market correction would likely require a slowdown in cash flows and capex that underpin valuations. Higher rates and geopolitics are not seen as likely to derail AI.
Potential correction triggers named: serious competition against the largest AI names, GPU competition, a sharp fall in memory prices that compresses margins, and regulatory intervention.

Forward valuations of AI-related tech names carry little premium, which participants attribute to skepticism, fear of job displacement and doubts about returns on capital. The test given is whether hyperscaler ROIC exceeds cost of capital in three years.

AI investment has offset part of the drag from higher rates. If it moderates, the economy shifts back toward consumption (about 70% of GDP), which is vulnerable if AI displaces labor faster than new jobs form.

Concentration: AI exposure runs through public and private markets, investment-grade credit, energy, inflation and Fed policy, so a clean hedge is hard to build. NEPC would advocate diversifying S&P 500 exposure if the top 10 exceed 50% of the index. The top 5 are currently above 25%.
Beyond AI: equal-weighted S&P 500 earnings grew double digits over the past 12 months and are expected to continue. Small and mid caps could benefit if rate pressure eases.
Portfolio stance: let AI winners run, rebalance into Treasuries when equity exposure breaches the upper end of target ranges, and stay overweight equities versus targets with risk controls.

Energy: Jennifer calls an Iran-US driven energy crisis an underappreciated risk. Buffers such as reserves are thinning and Middle East infrastructure is under pressure. She expects demand destruction to limit the inflationary effect, and notes China returning to the market.

Emerging markets: Taiwan and Korea are over 50% of the index and three names are 27%. Participants recommend active management and see EM as a poor diversifier from the Magnificent 7. Active extension strategies are being considered in both US and EM.
2027 forces named: interest rates and Treasury yields amid government spending, private-market exits and distributions, AI monetization, politics, the Fed and geopolitics/energy.

Biggest mispriced risk per James: concern over Fed independence has pushed rates too high, and he would stay long equities as it prices out. Phillip says yields are up on higher real rates, not inflation expectations, and expects rates to fall somewhat. He sees US corporate growth as the most mispriced item.
Robert flags that high rates and AI financing needs could crowd out other sectors and slow private markets. James says overleveraged AI deals with weak customers failing is acceptable.
Core fixed income and US equities are described as more attractive than in many years (S&P 500 and Bloomberg Aggregate).

2027 top asset class picks: long credit (James), US small caps (Jennifer), US tech (Michael), Bitcoin as a crypto proxy (Robert), Nasdaq (Phillip), US equities (Christopher). Phillip expects episodic volatility spikes.

sector_views.sector: US small and mid cap equities
sector_views.rationale: Could benefit if upward pressure on interest rates moderates. Jennifer picks US small caps as the 2027 top asset class.
Forward P/E multiples look somewhat attractive after the pressure on large-cap tech. Michael and Phillip pick US tech and Nasdaq for 2027.
Index is heavily concentrated in AI-linked Taiwan and Korea, so it does not diversify away from the Magnificent 7. Active management is favored.
Described as more attractive than in many years, and Treasuries are viewed as a safe haven and a rebalancing destination.

earnings_insights: Equal-weighted S&P 500 earnings grew at a double-digit rate over the past 12 months and are expected to continue over the next 12 months (Phillip).
Memory earnings growth is expected to moderate as new competitors enter, though not disappear (Jennifer).

macro_indicators.interpretation: Consumer demand would carry more of growth if AI investment moderates.

macro_indicators.reading: higher on real rates, not inflation expectations
macro_indicators.interpretation: Phillip attributes the rise to higher real rates, reflecting either strong growth or a higher risk premium.
Markets have waited for this dislocation this year. Jennifer says demand destruction would limit the inflationary effect.

crypto_views: Robert picks cryptocurrency, using Bitcoin as a proxy, as his top-performing asset class for 2027.

trade_ideas.description: Overweight US equities versus targets, rebalancing trims into Treasuries when exposure exceeds the upper end of the target range
trade_ideas.rationale: Treasury yields are attractive and AI leaders are liquid and easy to rebalance.

trade_ideas.description: Long US small and mid cap equities if interest rate pressure moderates
trade_ideas.rationale: Small and mid caps have been pressured by higher rates and could benefit when that eases.

trade_ideas.description: Active extension (long-short) strategies in US and EM equities
trade_ideas.rationale: They allow managers to identify over- or under-valued mid and small-cap AI names while holding large-cap exposure in concentrated markets.

tension_points.bull_case: Robert argues productivity gains may bring a shorter workweek and labor shortages instead of job losses. Phillip says new technology creates new industries and jobs.
tension_points.bear_case: Christopher and James say gains from a falling labor share or displacement without new job creation could weigh on household income and consumption.
tension_points.what_invalidates: AI job displacement not offset by new business formation and job creation.

tension_points.bull_case: Phillip says return on equity remains high across technology companies and investment is still insufficient relative to the opportunity.
tension_points.bear_case: Robert and Jennifer question the capital intensity and balance sheets of AI spenders and the sustainability of memory earnings.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Hyperscaler return on invested capital falling below cost of capital within three years.

tension_points.bull_case: James says high rates may be fleeting and do not impair AI economics because deals are financed against growth multiples.
tension_points.bear_case: Robert says high rates and AI financing needs may crowd out other sectors and slow private markets.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Rates staying high enough that deal NPVs no longer work.
